# Cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitor-associated thromboembolism: a critical evaluation of the current evidence

**Authors:** Nathan W. Watson; Joseph J. Shatzel; Hanny Al-Samkari

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2Division of Hematology and Oncology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Knight Cancer Institute, Oregon Health and Sciences University, Portland, Oregon, USA | 4Division of Biomedical Engineering, Oregon Health and Sciences University, Portland, Oregon, USA

## Abstract

Cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK 4/6) inhibitors are an essential treatment modality for hormone receptor–positive breast cancer. As the rates of breast cancer continue to rise globally and the indications for CDK 4/6 inhibitors now extend beyond metastatic disease, more patients than ever are receiving these agents. Thrombosis is an emerging clinical concern with this class of agents, particularly venous thromboembolism. Although venous thromboembolism initially emerged as an adverse effect of interest in early trials, more recent studies have demonstrated even higher incidences of thrombosis in real-world clinical practice. In this review, we summarize the evidence to date that has informed the thrombosis risk for these agents both in clinical trials and real-world studies. We review data describing the venous and arterial thromboembolic risks in clinical trials of CDK 4/6 inhibitors as well as the now rather extensive real-world evidence available, including a comparison of risk for each of the 3 agents approved for use in breast cancer: palcociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib. As the role of prophylactic anticoagulation continues to remain unknown in women receiving CDK 4/6 inhibitors, future efforts directed at carefully investigating the risks and benefits of thromboprophylaxis may lead to improved outcomes in these patients.

## INTRODUCTION

Over the past decade, cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 (CDK 4/6) inhibitors have become an essential frontline treatment for hormone receptor (HR)–positive breast cancer [1–3]. CDK4 and CDK6 are cell cycle kinases that function as regulators of cell cycle progression and are known to be particularly relevant to breast cancer pathogenesis [4–6]. As a cellular sensor, CDK 4/6 responds to signals in the extracellular environment via direct interactions with cyclin D1 [7,8]. These interactions lead to selective phosphorylation of the tumor suppressor Rb and thereby direct control over cellular progression from the G1 to S phase [9,10]. As such, it has been well established that inhibition of this pathway is a favorable treatment strategy for targeted breast cancer therapy [8,11].

The culmination of these early investigations was the successful 2015 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of the first CDK 4/6 inhibitor, palbociclib [12]. Palbociclib (Ibrance, Pfizer), a potent inhibitor of both proteins CDK4 and CDK6, was initially approved for postmenopausal women with HR–positive metastatic disease in combination with letrozole. However, palbociclib’s indication in the United States has further expanded to include combination therapy with fulvestrant in patients who have previously failed endocrine therapy. Two additional CDK4/6 inhibitors, abemaciclib (Verzenio, Eli Lily), and ribociclib (Kisqali, Novartis), have also reached market with similar indications in breast cancer [13]. Additionally, based on evidence from the recently completed monarchE trial and exceptional response as a monotherapy in phase 2 trials, abemaciclib is now also authorized for early-stage, high-risk breast cancer and use as a monotherapy [14–16].

As breast cancer is the most common malignancy in women and its rates continue to rise globally, CDK 4/6 inhibitor use is becoming increasingly more common [17–19]. The most frequently observed adverse effect for this class is neutropenia, which has resulted in a warning on the FDA label for all 3 approved agents [20–22]. However, in the past several years, it has become increasingly clear that CDK 4/6 inhibitors also have an increased risk of thrombosis, particularly venous thromboembolism (VTE) [23]. As with other targeted therapies [24], the mechanism of the prothrombotic nature of these agents largely remains unclear [25].

Although a signal for increased VTE risk was seen in early clinical trials, recent studies have demonstrated higher thromboembolic event rates in real-world clinical practice [26–28]. Additionally, post approval studies have also suggested a possible arterial thrombosis risk associated with these agents [27,29]. These data raise the question of whether a certain CDK 4/6 inhibitor may be more thrombogenic than others, an issue particularly salient in high-risk populations (which were largely excluded from clinical trials). As it remains unclear whether thrombosis is a side effect of the entire medication class or whether rates differ between individual agents, no studies to date have specifically compared the existing data to better elucidate this difference. In this narrative review, we seek to summarize the existing literature to evaluate both the clinical trial evidence and real-world data of VTE and arterial thrombosis associated with each of the CDK 4/6 inhibitors as well as provide insight and direction for future investigation.

## PALBOCICLIB

Palbociclib was the first CDK 4/6 inhibitor to reach the market in the United States via data from the PALOMA family of clinical trials [30]. The initial trial in the series, PALOMA 1, was a phase 2 study that investigated palbociclib in combination with letrozole as a firstline agent for HR–positive breast cancer [31,32]. Importantly, this study demonstrated approximately a 10-month increase in progression-free survival with the addition of palbociclib to letrozole as the firstline agent in metastatic disease. Palbociclib was well tolerated with reported adverse events generally consistent with that of CDK 4/6 inhibitors as a class, namely, hematologic toxicity. The most commonly observed adverse events included neutropenia (74% of patients), leukopenia (43% of patients), and fatigue (40% of patients) [31]. Patients who had a history of a major cardiovascular event within the prior 6 months were excluded from this trial. This study was also the first to reveal a signal of increased thromboembolism risk for palbociclib. Four of 83 enrolled participants in the palbociclib plus letrozole arm (5%) developed a pulmonary embolism (PE) while on therapy, 3 of which were considered serious adverse events. Patients received palbociclib for a median of 13.8 months in this study (Table 1) [33]. By comparison, no serious adverse events, including thromboembolic complications, were reported in more than 1 patient in the letrozoleonly arm (Table 1) [31]. Data from this trial subsequently led to palbociclib’s approval in 2015 with an associated warning for VTE (which was later removed based on results of the PALOMA 2 and 3 studies).

PALOMA-2 confirmed and expanded upon the encouraging findings observed in the phase 2 trials for palbociclib and letrozole as a firstline combination for advanced disease. Similarly, patients were excluded from this study if they had any major cardiovascular events within 6 months of enrollment. Among the 444 patients who received palbociclib, a similar adverse event profile was seen; however, rates of VTE were not quite as high as was seen in the phase 2 studies. The incidence of VTE in PALOMA-2 was 1.4% over a median duration of treatment of 19.8 months, consisting mostly of PEs (0.9% of patients receiving palbociclib) (Table 1) [34]. One patient receiving palbociclib had an arterial thrombotic event (thrombotic stroke) (Table 2). No arterial thromboses were observed in the placebo arm. Similar rates of thrombosis were observed in PALOMA-3, which enrolled patients who had previously progressed on standard-of-care endocrine therapy and investigated palbociclib with fulvestrant [35,36]. PALOMA-3 had similar exclusion criteria as the prior trials. In this more heavily pretreated population, 5 patients (1.4%) developed a total of 6 VTE events (1.7%) over a median treatment duration of 7.63 months, of which 4 met the criteria for serious adverse events [37].

In a safety analysis pooling data from the PALOMA-1, -2, and -3 trials, which included 5 years of follow-up, a rate of 2.25 VTE events per 100 person-years was reported for palbociclib plus endocrine therapy [38]. Over half of these events were PE with a rate of 1.27 events per 100 person-years. As compared with placebo, VTE and PE had hazard ratios of 1.3 (95% CI, 0.6–2.9) and 1.4 (95% CI, 0.5–3.9) (both not statistically significant), respectively [38].

The more recently launched PALLAS trial, a multinational, multicenter, phase 3 study, also assessed palbociclib in combination with adjuvant endocrine therapy, but this time for early-stage breast cancer. Although still ongoing, at the second planned interim analysis, these results indicated that palbociclib did not improve invasive disease-free survival compared with endocrine therapy alone [39]. However, among the 2883 patients with less advanced disease recruited to receive palbociclib, VTE prevalence was similar to that seen in the PALOMA-2 and PALOMA-3 studies at 1.6%, despite enrolling a healthier cohort of patients with less advanced disease (Table 1). Notably, unlike PALOMA-2 and PALOMA-3, patients received either an aromatase inhibitor or tamoxifen in combination with palbociclib in the PALLAS trial.

Although a modest VTE–palbociclib association was initially established in the sanitized populations of randomized clinical trials, the evidence that followed from real-world populations has raised the level of concern over this morbid and potentially fatal complication considerably. The first such study was a small single-center, observational retrospective analysis of patients receiving palbociclib at their practice over a 6-month period. Among the 64 patients included in this analysis, 7 patients (10.9%) developed VTE on palbociclib. Of note, 6 of these events were of grade 2 severity and 1 was of grade 3 (a saddle PE) [40].

Evidence from this small study was soon followed by evidence from larger studies. Gervaso et al. [26] performed a single-center, observational retrospective cohort study of 424 patients treated with CDK 4/6 inhibitors, of whom 92% received palbociclib. With a much larger patient cohort, this study found a 9.0% VTE incidence during palbociclib treatment or within 30 days of its discontinuation (Table 1). The most common event reported was deep vein thrombosis (DVT), occurring in 18 patients (4.2%). Survival was numerically, although not statistically significantly, lower in patients experiencing VTE [26].

Following this study, the thromboembolism risk of palbociclib was further assessed by West et al. [27] in a 2021 study. This group conducted a multicenter, observational retrospective cohort study evaluating both venous and arterial thrombosis incidence in patients with metastatic breast cancer receiving one of the CDK 4/6 inhibitors. They included 266 total patients, of whom 89% received palbociclib. Similar to the 2 prior studies, this study found a VTE incidence much higher than reported in clinical trials, with 21 total events (7.9%) being observed in their cohort during treatment or within 30 days of discontinuation. Patients received therapy for a median of 10.9 months. Additionally, this group also notably found an arterial thrombosis incidence of 4.1%, much higher than any palbociclib clinical trial (Table 1). Similar to prior studies, the most common VTE event was DVT (Table 2) [27].

## RIBOCICLIB

Ribociclib is the second CDK 4/6 inhibitor that has been approved for use in the United States. Based on data from the MONALEESA trial program [41,42], ribociclib is approved for use in postmenopausal women in combination with fulvestrant as initial therapy or following progression on endocrine therapy as well as in pre-/perimenopausal women with an aromatase inhibitor [43]. Similar to other CDK 4/6 inhibitors, the most common adverse effects reported with ribociclib include neutropenia, nausea, and fatigue [44].

The phase 3 MONALEESA-2 trial investigated ribociclib in combination with letrozole as firstline therapy for metastatic breast cancer. Similar to previous studies investigating this combination with other CDK 4/6 inhibitors, progression-free survival was shown to be improved significantly with the addition of ribociclib when compared with placebo (HR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.43–0.72) [45]. MONALEESA-3 excluded patients with clinically significant cardiovascular disease or prior major cardiovascular events within 12 months of study entry. Although ribociclib was well tolerated, approximately twice the number of serious adverse events was reported with this agent relative to placebo (21.3% vs. 11.8%). Among these serious adverse events, 7.5% versus 1.5% were directly attributed to ribociclib and placebo, respectively. Regarding thromboembolic events, only 2 PEs (0.6%) were reported in this study, both of which were in the ribociclib arm. Patients received ribociclib for a median of 13 months [46,47].

MONALEESA-3 and MONALEESA-7 further explored ribociclib for additional indications [41,48]. MONALEESA-3 was a phase 3 study investigating ribociclib with fulvestrant in postmenopausal women [49,50]. Relative to MONALEESA-2, considerably more patients developed VTE than previously observed. Among patients receiving ribociclib, 27 (5.6%) developed PE. However, 15 patients (6.2%) receiving a placebo also were diagnosed with PE [51]. One patient receiving ribociclib died as a result of venous thrombosis [49]. A similarly high rate of VTE was also seen in MONALEESA-7 [52]. A total of 10 PEs and 1 cerebral venous thrombosis were reported for patients receiving ribociclib over a nearly 2-year treatment duration (3.3% of patients treated with ribociclib). However, unlike MONALEESA-3, only 3 patients (0.9%) receiving a placebo had a VTE. Moreover, unique to this trial were arterial thrombosis events attributed to ribociclib. Two arterial thromboses (0.6%) were reported including 1 stroke (0.3%) and 1 acute coronary event (0.3%) [46,53].

In 2022, Abdel-Razeq et al. [54] reported on the thromboembolism rates of patients in the first significant real-world cohort of patients with breast cancer receiving ribociclib. This study included 305 patients, all of whom had metastatic disease at the time of initiating ribociclib in combination with endocrine therapy. They observed only 6 confirmed thromboembolic events (2.0%) during ribociclib therapy or within 30 days of discontinuation; 5 of these events were VTE (1.6%) and 1 was an arterial thrombosis (0.3%). Patients in this study received ribociclib for a median of 8 months. Among the VTEs, 2 (0.7%) were cerebral venous sinus thromboses and 3 were PEs (1.0%). The single arterial thrombotic event reported was a peripheral artery thrombosis manifesting clinically as acute limb ischemia (Table 2) [54].

## ABEMACICLIB

As compared with palbociclib and ribociclib, abemaciclib is a structurally unique CDK 4/6 inhibitor [55]. In preclinical studies, abemaciclib was shown to be 14-fold more selective for CDK4 than CDK6, in vitro [56,57]. Abemaciclib has a similar toxicity profile as its predecessors, consisting mostly of neutropenia, fatigue, and nausea [58]. Unique to abemaciclib, and possibly related to its structural differences, is gastrointestinal toxicity with diarrhea reported very frequently in phase 3 studies [59,60].

MONARCH 1 was the first study to formally investigate abemaciclib in patients with metastatic breast cancer [61]. In this phase 2 study, abemaciclib was investigated as a monotherapy in HR+/HER2− advanced disease. Among the 132 patients recruited, VTE was an infrequent adverse event, occurring in only 1 patient [16,62] (Table 2). However, VTE incidence was higher in phase 3 studies, occurring in 21 (4.8%) and 20 (6.1%) patients in MONARCH 2 and MONARCH 3, respectively (Table 1) [59,60,63]. The median duration of abemaciclib therapy in these studies was 14 and 14.9 months, respectively. As with trials for other agents, patients in MONARCH-2 and -3 were excluded if there was a personal history of recent cardiovascular events. In MONARCH 2, 8 thrombotic events (1.8%) were considered serious with 19 out of 21 patients requiring therapeutic anticoagulation. Similarly, in MONARCH 3, 9 events (2.8%) were considered serious with 3 patient deaths (0.9%) attributed to VTE [58]. The results of these pivotal trials and notably the deaths reported in MONARCH 3 led to a black box warning for VTE on the abemaciclib FDA label.

More recently, monarchE investigated abemaciclib with standard-of-care adjuvant endocrine therapy for use in early-stage high-risk breast cancer. Patients in this study were recruited based on the presence of tumor features indicating high-risk disease including axillary lymph node involvement, high Ki-67 proliferation index, and tumor size. In the 2808 patients randomized to receive abemaciclib, 63 total VTE events (2.2%) were reported (Table 2). In comparison, only 14 VTE events (0.5%) occurred in patients receiving endocrine therapy only. Of note, 30.7% of patients receiving abemaciclib were also concurrently taking tamoxifen rather than an aromatase inhibitor. No arterial events were reported in this study [14,15]. MONARCH-plus was also recently completed and specifically looked at abemaciclib with endocrine therapy in patients living in China, Brazil, India, and South Africa. Similar to monarchE, a VTE incidence of 2.6% was reported in this study. Of note, 3 arterial thromboses each presenting as a peripheral artery occlusive event also occurred (1.0%, Table 2) [25,64,65].

In 2022, Watson et al. [28] reported the first study investigating the real-world rates of VTE and arterial thrombosis in a patient receiving abemaciclib therapy. This multicenter, observational cohort study investigated 364 patients diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer and were treated with abemaciclib. This study found that 7.4% of patients developed a thrombotic event during treatment or within 30 days of discontinuation. Patients received abemaciclib therapy for a median duration of 6.5 months. VTE was the most common thrombotic event observed occurring in 4.7% of patients, followed by arterial thrombosis in 2.5% of patients. Notably, this study demonstrated that patients who developed VTE while on abemaciclib therapy also had a greater risk of death [28,66].

## DISCUSSION

Considerable data is now available regarding CDK 4/6 inhibitor-associated thromboembolism in patients with breast cancer. Figure 1 summarizes the event rates calculated in person-years for each of the major trials and real-world studies investigating each CDK 4/6 inhibitor to date.

Regarding VTE risk, real-world rates of VTE were increased when compared with the reported clinical trial rates for all 3 of the CDK 4/6 inhibitors. Notably, the agent which had the greatest increased risk was palbociclib, which had a VTE rate of 0.8 to 4.1 per 100 person-years in clinical trials and 8.7 per 100 person-years in the real-world setting representing approximately a 2.1- to 10.9-fold increase (Table 1) [32]. Abemaciclib demonstrated the highest rate of VTE in clinical trials (1.8–4.9 events per 100 person-years) [56]. These rates were primarily defined by the MONARCH 2 and 3 studies, which consequently earned this agent a black box warning by the FDA [59,60,63]. Conversely, among the studies conducted within the real-world practice, ribociclib had the lowest risk of VTE. In evidence published in a study performed by Abdel-Rzeq et al. [54] (in 2022), the rate of VTE among patients treated with ribociclib was 1.6% or 2.5 events per 100 person-years (Table 1, Figure 2).

Although these low rates of thrombosis with ribociclib are encouraging, additional data are necessary to determine whether this agent has a lower thrombosis risk profile as compared with other CDK 4/6 inhibitors. There are several limitations of the Abdel-Rzeq study that may prevent the generalizability of the results. First, the median age of the cohort was just 49 years, representing a younger cohort when compared with the MONALEESA trials, which had a pooled median age of 58 years [44]. It is well recognized that age is an extremely important risk factor for both venous and arterial thrombosis. Moreover, unlike large real-world evidence studies of palbociclib and abemaciclib reporting much higher VTE rates than in clinical trials [27,28], this study also did not report on any concurrent VTE or arterial thrombosis risk factors to characterize the baseline risk among patients in their study or specify baseline use of antithrombotic agents. Additionally, as ribociclib concurrently carries a risk for QT interval prolongation and requires standing electrocardiographic monitoring during therapy, a selection bias for patients with limited cardiac comorbidities may also exist for ribociclib in clinical practice [67]. Nonetheless, this reduced thromboembolism rate in a real-world cohort merits additional study and potential confirmation.

A recent study attempted to further characterize and compare the rates of thromboembolism among the 3 approved agents utilizing the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System, a database composed of voluntarily reported drug-related events submitted to the US FDA [68]. This group queried this database for all adverse events caused by the CDK 4/6 inhibitors and utilized a disproportionality screening analysis to assess for any signal of increased VTE. In contrast to other studies, this approach found that all CDK 4/6 inhibitors and specifically palbociclib and ribociclib had a stronger signal for increased VTE as compared with abemaciclib. However, given the nature of the study design, the ability to assess causal relationships is limited [68]. Thein et al. [69] (in 2020) also published a meta-analysis synthesizing data from the PALOMA, MONALEESA, and MONARCH clinical trials to characterize the risk profiles determined in trials and compare individual agents, finding a 2.6-fold increase in VTE when a CDK 4/6 inhibitor was added to endocrine therapy. In subgroup analysis, abemaciclib was the only agent found to have a statistically significant increased risk of VTE, whereas the risk increase with palbociclib and ribociclib was not significant [69]. A more recent meta-analysis adding data from newer studies additionally found a 2- to 3-fold increase in venous and arterial thrombosis risk with the addition of a CDK 4/6 inhibitor. However, this work did not compare individual agents [70].

Although VTE risk was well documented in trials, arterial thrombosis appears to be an emerging clinical concern predominantly seen in the real-world setting. Arterial thrombosis was a rare adverse event reported within clinical trials, with ischemic stroke being the most common event reported (Figure 3). However, as clinical trials select groups of patients with limited comorbidities, it is not surprising to find higher real-world rates of arterial thrombosis in unselected populations. In our analysis of the published literature, arterial thrombosis rates appear to be several-fold higher in real-world practice for all 3 CDK 4/6 inhibitors (Figure 2). In one real-world study investigating thrombosis in patients receiving abemaciclib, the authors report 5.1 arterial thromboses per 100 person-years, representing a greater than 2.8-fold increase compared with the trials investigating abemaciclib (Figure 2). This increase was attributed to the high rates of cardiovascular risk factors present at baseline among the women who were enrolled in their cohort [28].

As CDK 4/6 inhibitors are frequently utilized in combination with aromatase inhibitors and selective estrogen modulators, the thrombosis risk for various dual-therapy regimens is an important consideration. However, evidence comparing thrombosis rates between individual endocrine therapies is lacking. In a phase 3 study comparing fulvestrant alone versus anastrozole alone in patients with HR− positive advanced disease, there was no difference in VTE rates between groups (0.4% vs. 0.4%) [71]. However, in a more recent study investigating palbociclib–fulvestrant versus palbociclib–letrozole in a similar patient population, the rates of PE were 5.0% and 2.5%, respectively [72]. Although it is possible that the addition of CDK 4/6 inhibitor to fulvestrant might be more thrombogenic than the addition of CDK 4/6 inhibitor to letrozole, more data are necessary to further investigate this association. Furthermore, the thrombosis risk in malignancies beyond breast cancer also remains ill defined. In the phase III JUNIPER study, patients with metastatic non–small cell lung carcinoma who had previously failed platinum-based chemotherapy were randomized to receive either abemaciclib or the epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor, erlotinib. Venous thromboembolic events were reported in 1.9% of patients treated with abemaciclib versus 1.1% in patients receiving erlotinib [73]. Additionally, in patients with advanced esophageal or gastric cancer receiving palbociclib, as many as 10% of patients enrolled in 1 phase II study experienced a thromboembolic event [74]. This early evidence suggests that an increased thromboembolism risk of these agents may exist irrespective of tumor type.

Moreover, although a plethora of clinical data have emerged documenting thrombosis in populations receiving CDK 4/6 inhibitors, no studies to date have specifically investigated the potential mechanism of this prothrombotic state. Previous work by Dunbar et al. [75] (in 2021) found that patients with CDKN2B mutations have a 1.45-fold increase in cancer-associated thromboembolism [76]. This association may explain why CDK 4/6-blockade also leads to increased rates of thromboembolism, although more research is necessary to work out this mechanism. Moreover, other therapies targeting growth factor–related pathways such as the anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) antiangiogenics have also been implicated with increased thromboembolic rates and their mechanisms have been postulated to be related to their effect on endothelial cell survival and consequential vascular injury [24,77]. Possible mechanistic similarities may exist for the CDK 4/6 inhibitors.

To our knowledge, no studies to date have been conducted investigating thromboprophylaxis among breast cancer patients receiving CDK 4/6 inhibitors. However, thromboprophylaxis has been thoroughly investigated for cancer-associated thrombosis as well as for other treatment-associated thrombosis syndromes. To date, numerous clinical trials have investigated VTE prophylaxis for ambulatory cancer patients [78,79]. For example, the CONKO-004 trial assessed enoxaparin in patients with locally advanced or metastatic pancreatic cancer and found nearly a 9% reduction in the cumulative incidence of VTE [80]. Similarly, the more recent AVERT trial has further validated prophylactic-dose apixaban to also effectively reduce VTE risk in ambulatory cancer patients [81,82].

In addition to anticoagulant thromboprophylaxis, antiplatelet strategies such as the administration of low-dose aspirin, an antithrombotic agent, are effective in patients with multiple myeloma. Because immunomodulatory agents, including thalidomide and its derivatives, have been strongly associated with VTE, particularly when combined with corticosteroids in patients with multiple myeloma [24], thromboprophylaxis is currently the standard of care. A phase 3 trial investigating warfarin, low–molecular weight heparin (LMWH), and aspirin for use as a prophylactic antithrombotic agent in patients receiving thalidomide-containing regimens found LMWH and aspirin fairly equivalent and more effective than warfarin at preventing the primary composite endpoint of serious thromboembolic events, acute cardiovascular events, or sudden death [83]. Additionally, head-to-head comparisons between aspirin and LWMH have shown no differences in both thrombosis and bleeding rates in this population [84]. Given the apparent success of aspirin prophylaxis in myeloma, similar approaches may find an application in patients treated with CDK 4/6 inhibitors.

As numerous studies have evaluated thromboprophylaxis for cancer patients in the ambulatory setting, extrapolating these findings to CDK 4/6 inhibitor-associated thromboembolism could serve as a starting point for future thromboprophylaxis investigations. Currently, the biggest limitation for this population is the lack of a validated risk score to predict patients at risk for VTE. Traditionally, patients at risk for cancer-associated thrombosis have been risk stratified via risk prediction scores such as the Khorana risk score [85,86]. However, 2 studies have attempted to utilize the Khorana risk score to predict for thrombosis in breast cancer patients receiving CDK 4/6 inhibitors, showing poor predictive power of the score in this population [27,28]. West et al. [25] (in 2022) recently proposed the use of breast tumor somatic mutations to create an individualized VTE risk assessment for these patients, although no such tool has currently been validated. Future work directed at more adequate risk stratification for these patients is certainly necessary.

Although thromboprophylaxis may benefit a particular subset of patients receiving treatment with a CDK 4/6 inhibitor, dedicated studies are required to carefully balance the bleeding and thrombotic risk in this population. As major bleeding can also be a problem in cancer patients [87,88], low-risk bleeding agents such as low-dose aspirin or prophylactic-dose direct oral anticoagulants may be a reasonable choice for future study [89].

## CONCLUSIONS

As CDK 4/6 inhibitors are a mainstay treatment for metastatic and now early-stage breast cancer, it is time to address the risk of CDK 4/6 inhibitor-associated thrombosis. We have a large body of evidence suggesting an increased risk of thrombosis in patients receiving these agents—a risk that appears to be even higher in real-world settings than what was initially reported in clinical trials. The risk elevation is clearest for venous thrombosis but may exist for arterial thrombosis as well, particularly given the findings in real-world studies. It is not clear yet whether thromboembolic risk differs between agents. However, while risk profiles were similar on the whole in the clinical trial setting, real-world evidence suggests potentially higher risk with abemaciclib and palbociclib over ribociclib. Future studies must answer this outstanding question and assess the value of thromboprophylaxis, ideally in those patients with the highest thrombotic risk.
